name: SOC Detection Lab - Coverage
description: Techniques with detection rules written and tested in this lab. Score 100 = high confidence, low false positive rate, used as a live alert. Score 50 = rule written and documented but not reliable standalone, used as an input to a correlated detection instead.

techniques.comment: Detects download cradles, encoded commands, hidden windows and script file loading. Tuned from 4 hits to 2, both from the test, by removing bare Import-Module and requiring http alongside IEX and Invoke-Expression.

Detected two ways: wevtutil and Clear-EventLog process creation, plus System Event ID 104 which Windows writes when a log is cleared. Zero false positives. Reading logs does not match, only clearing them.

Sysmon Event ID 13, registry writes to Run and RunOnce. Tuned from 7 hits to 1. False positives were Microsoft Edge autolaunch and rundll32 GrpConv, excluded on full path plus value name plus account rather than process name.
Covers schtasks.exe /create and the PowerShell scheduled task cmdlets. Reading tasks does not match. Caught a task created with /ru system, which is privilege escalation as well as persistence.

Sysmon process creation plus Security Event ID 4720 and 4732. The Security events were missing until the User Account Management audit subcategory was enabled. The detection gap was telemetry, not query logic.

Written but not viable as a standalone alert. 21 hits in a near-idle lab, and systeminfo run by an attacker is identical to systeminfo run by an admin. Used as an input to the discovery burst correlation.
Same limitation as T1082. 19 hits, and no field distinguishes malicious from routine use of whoami. Feeds the discovery burst correlation.
5 hits. The timing was the useful finding: four network commands from one cmd.exe inside 240ms is scripted, not typed. That observation led to the discovery burst rule.
